background: Between 1865 and 1970 the American economy was repeatedly transformed: a continental railroad network was completed, industrial capitalism concentrated production in cities, panics and depressions (1873, 1893, 1929) dislocated millions, wartime mobilization reshaped labor markets twice, and post–World War II prosperity rebuilt the middle class. Each of these economic shifts moved people.
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which changes in the American economy influenced patterns of internal migration in the United States in the period from 1865 to 1970.
exemplar_thesis: Economic change was the dominant driver of internal migration between 1865 and 1970: railroads and industrial jobs pulled immigrants and rural migrants to cities; depression-era collapse pushed Okies west and Black Southerners north; wartime production created the Great Migration's jobs and the Sunbelt's defense boom; and postwar prosperity, highways, and air conditioning made the Sunbelt's growth self-reinforcing. While racism, federal policy, and war itself shaped where people could go, the economy determined when and why they moved.
rubric: LEQ 6-point rubric (Fall 2026 CED): (1) Thesis — historically defensible claim establishing a line of reasoning about the extent of economic influence on migration (1 pt). (2) Contextualization — broader context, e.g., Reconstruction's labor systems; the closing of the frontier; Cold War defense spending (1 pt). (3) Evidence — at least 2 specific examples (1 pt); evidence effectively supports an argument responding to the prompt (1 pt). (4) Analysis and reasoning — historical reasoning (causation, continuity/change) used to structure the argument (1 pt); complexity — e.g., qualifying the economic argument with non-economic factors (racism, policy, war), or tracing migration chains across sub-periods (1 pt).
suggested_evidence_areas: Railroads and western settlement: Homestead Act (1862), transcontinental lines, and mining/ranching booms drawing settlers west after 1865.
Urban industrialization: factory and tenement cities pulling European immigrants and rural Americans eastward and northward, 1870–1910.

The Great Migration (c. 1916–1970): Black Southerners moving to northern and western industrial centers during both world wars' labor shortages, pushed also by Jim Crow and agricultural mechanization.
Depression-era displacement: Dust Bowl 'Okies' migrating to California; New Deal programs (e.g., TVA, CCC) relocating workers.
Wartime economies: World War II defense plants drawing workers to the West Coast and the Sunbelt; the Bracero Program (1942–1964) as managed labor migration.
Postwar Sunbelt growth: defense spending, air conditioning, highways, and service economies pulling population south and west after 1945.
